subject: Function to Account for Seeing the Same Species Multiple Times?

messages.author: 293d911d5114407e
messages.subject: Function to Account for Seeing the Same Species Multiple Times?
parts:
Hi Everyone!

I was wondering if there is a function that could be applied that will account for the possibility of seeing the same species more than once in order to increase the accuracy of abundance estimates. Thanks!

Nicole

messages.author: 75e0b0abcbafbc7d
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Function to Account for Seeing the Same Species Multiple Times?
parts:
Nicole


Not quite sure what you are asking--do you mean possibility seeing the same *individual* multiple times during a survey?


If that is what you are asking, I presume you would need some type of movement model.  There are some such models, but none that are sufficiently generic to alter accuracy of estimates.

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] Function to Account for Seeing the Same Species Multiple Times?
parts:
If you see the same individual multiple times because you traverse lines multiple times, then the method accounts for that.  Lines (or points) are assumed to be independent, but multiple traverses of the same line are not assumed to be independent.  If you see the same animal multiple times on the same traverse, and you record it as a new detection each time, then you will over-estimate abundance.  If you can identify individuals, then you could incorporate a movement model to exploit the multiple sightings.  I find it difficult to see that there would be much benefit if any of doing so.  To develop an appropriate model, you would need to distinguish the case of the multiple detections being due to chance, from the case that the multiple detections are because an individual animal is responding to you.  Richard Glennie at St Andrews has developed movement models for distance sampling, but not for this purpose – his methods adjust for bias when movement of animals is not slow relative to movement of the observer.

 

Steve Buckland
